name: Balixafortide
status: Not FDA-approved; the phase 3 FORTRESS trial in breast cancer was stopped in 2021 after missing its main goal
mechanism: Designed to block the CXCR4 receptor that helps cancer and immune cells move and settle in tissues, with the aim of making chemotherapy work better
uses: Studied in HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer

article.summary: Balixafortide is an experimental CXCR4-blocking peptide tested with the chemotherapy eribulin in metastatic breast cancer. The phase 3 FORTRESS trial showed no benefit, and it is not approved.
article.takeaway: Balixafortide is an experimental intravenous peptide that blocks CXCR4, a receptor involved in how cancer cells and immune cells move through and settle in tissues. In a phase 1 trial, **30%** of 54 evaluable women with heavily pretreated metastatic breast cancer responded to balixafortide plus the chemotherapy eribulin.[^1] The larger phase 3 FORTRESS trial then failed: response rates were **13.0%** with the combination and **13.7%** with eribulin alone, and the study was terminated for missing its primary endpoint.[^2][^3] The drug is not FDA-approved for any use.
glance: Investigational; phase 3 trial failed and a follow-on trial was withdrawn
HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, combined with eribulin
IV infusion on several days of each 21-day chemotherapy cycle
Phase 1 (56 patients) and phase 3 FORTRESS (432 patients)

blocks.text: CXCR4 is a receptor on many cell types that responds to a signaling protein called CXCL12. The pair helps steer immune cells, keeps blood stem cells in the bone marrow, and has been linked in cancer to tumor spread and to a tumor's surroundings that shield it from treatment. In laboratory models, CXCR4 blockers made several anticancer treatments work better, which is the idea behind balixafortide.[^1][^4]
A related blocker, [motixafortide](/peptides/motixafortide), is approved for a different job: releasing stem cells from bone marrow for collection before a transplant.

Balixafortide was developed by the Swiss company Polyphor, later renamed Spexis. After an early dose-finding study, the company ran FORTRESS (NCT03786094), a randomized phase 3 trial comparing balixafortide plus eribulin with eribulin alone in HER2-negative, locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer. It started in May 2019, enrolled 432 patients and was terminated in October 2021.[^2]
A later phase 1/2 trial of balixafortide with nab-paclitaxel or eribulin, sponsored by MedSIR, was withdrawn on a funder decision.[^5] The drug has no approved use.

blocks.text: The registry record gives the reason for stopping as failure to meet the primary endpoint.[^2] A response rate from a single-arm phase 1 trial cannot show what an added drug contributes, which is exactly what the randomized trial then tested.

items: **Common adverse events in phase 1:** fatigue (79%), neutropenia (57%), infusion-related reactions (48%), hair loss and constipation (46% each) and nausea (45%).[^1]
**Serious adverse events** in 38% of patients, including febrile neutropenia in 9%. Two of 56 patients died while on treatment, one from septic shock and one from pneumonia.[^1]
**Early dosing change:** a treatment-related death in the first cohort led investigators to redesign the schedule.[^1]

blocks.text: The phase 1 authors judged the combination's safety similar to that of eribulin or balixafortide alone. Much of the toxicity seen is typical of chemotherapy, so a randomized comparison is needed to separate it from the added drug's effects.

Because the only large randomized trial missed its endpoint, balixafortide is unlikely to reach the market for breast cancer. Its sponsor began a strategic review of the company in mid-2021,[^3] and the follow-on trial never enrolled. This entry could not confirm a formal end to the program.
CXCR4 blockade itself remains an active research area in cancer, and the signaling axis is being studied across many tumor types.[^4]

evidence.label: Early signal, then a failed phase 3 trial
evidence.text: Single-arm phase 1 results looked promising, but the randomized phase 3 trial showed no benefit over eribulin alone.[^1][^3] No other randomized data exist.

faq.a: No. The only large randomized trial, FORTRESS, did not show a benefit and was terminated early.[^2]

faq.q: How is it related to motixafortide?
faq.a: Both block CXCR4. [Motixafortide](/peptides/motixafortide) (Aphexda) is approved to mobilize stem cells in multiple myeloma, while balixafortide was tested as an add-on to chemotherapy in breast cancer.

faq.q: Why did phase 1 look better than phase 3?
faq.a: In phase 1 every patient received the combination, so it could not show what balixafortide added. In FORTRESS, patients on eribulin alone responded about as often (13.7%) as those who also received balixafortide (13.0%).[^3]
